# and `go tool coupling` measure: statement coverage restricted to the

column6: Every adapter crosses this. The core decides which operation fails; the adapter decides what failing means.
The sweep's own control flow: it decides whether the caller gets another pass.
The one adapter method returning another interface, so the only place injection can leak.
The error an adapter hands back, which the code under test applies predicates to.
The allocator boundary, and the outstanding count that crosses it.
The per-actor boundary: which role an operation belongs to is the adapter's judgement.
The byte count an adapter hands back with a partial failure. C4 covers the error; a caller acts on the count first, and under a short write it is neither 0 nor the whole buffer.

Run serves the check through this package's own fs.FS, and Recorder records through another. Both track that method set by hand, so a seek or a positional write added to fault/fs as an optional interface leaves every recorded offset wrong while the record stays internally consistent, and nothing here fails to build.

The list a caller asserts against to prove the sweep actually saw the file whose durability it is testing. The recorder decides what "served" means and the caller decides what "reached" means, so this is the one boundary where a green sweep and a meaningful sweep come apart. C8 covers the record itself; this covers the claim a reader makes about its completeness.

The adapter boundary for database/sql. The core decides which operation fails and this decides what failing means for a connection. It is also where the ErrBadConn decision is enforced: a tripped connect must not reach the base driver, and a retry inside database/sql is the only way it can.

The leak count crossing to the caller, and the analogue of C5 and fs.Outstanding. It is deliberately NOT sql.DB.Stats().OpenConnections, which counts what the pool holds rather than what this adapter handed out, and the difference between the two numbers is itself the finding.

The row rule, and the one boundary in this module where the operation count could come to depend on the DATA rather than on the structure of the code. Next consumes exactly one index for each result set, not one for each row. A mutant that made this fire when nothing was armed changed no test result, so it also carries the "does not invent a failure" property.

The optional-interface boundary of fork 3. database/sql type-asserts at run time and takes a different path on the answer, so a wrapper implementing fewer interfaces than the driver beneath it turns one driver call into three and moves every armed point after it. driver.ErrSkip is the documented way to decline without consuming an index.

The set a caller asserts against to prove a scenario stopped what it started, and the analogue of C9 for a resource no descriptor count can see. This package decides what "started since" means -- a delta against a snapshot, so leaks from an earlier sweep point are not charged to this one -- and the caller decides what "leaked" means, because a running worker belonging to an object still in use is not a leak. The two judgements are on opposite sides of this boundary, which is why it is a coupling rather than a return value. It is deliberately NOT a count: an absolute count is inherited by every later point of a sweep, and the harness that motivated this package reported 22 of 30 states leaking when the true figure was 4.

The Counter and Namer method sets crossing into this package: Outstanding, MaxOutstanding and OpenPaths decide what a leak check finds, and this package decides only how to word it. Report is the one site that reads every one of them.

The Delta method set crossing into this package: goroutine.Snapshot decides what "started since" means, per C14, and this function turns its answer into a per-goroutine test failure. A separate row from C15 because it reads a separate interface, at a separate call site. MEASURED 2026-09-02: 2 of 3 statements. Goroutines has three statements -- t.Helper(), the for-range over Since, and the t.Errorf inside its body -- and the t.Errorf is the one the profile never sees covered. TestGoroutinesPassesWhenNothingLeaked calls Goroutines directly, in-process, with an empty snapshot delta, so the profile sees t.Helper() and the zero-iteration loop but never enters the loop body. TestGoroutinesNamesEachLeakedGoroutine is the test that does reach the t.Errorf, but only inside a re-executed child process (leak/goroutines_test.go), started with exec.Command and no -test.coverprofile flag of its own, so whatever it runs is invisible to the parent's coverage profile. The same shape as go test's own -coverpkg finding in tools/coupling/measure.go: the statement runs, and the instrument that would see it is not the one watching.
